lead: Lighting turns geometry and light into a colour. It needs the surface normal, the direction to each light and the direction to the eye. Shading spreads that colour over a polygon. Gouraud computes light at the vertices and interpolates the colours. Phong interpolates the vertex normals, normalises them at each pixel and lights that pixel. The difference decides whether a shiny object shows a clean highlight or a dull smear. Games, CAD viewers and phone 3D apps choose between these costs every frame.
prereq: You need: face normals from Chapter 3.2 and visibility from Chapter 3.6.

blocks.text: Lighting starts from vectors, not pixels. At a surface point, N is the unit normal, L is the unit vector from the point towards a light, and V is the unit vector from the point towards the viewer. N·L is 1 when the surface faces the light directly and 0 at grazing light. Negative values mean the light is behind the surface and are clamped to 0. R is the mirror direction of L about N: R = 2(N·L)N − L. R·V is large when the eye lies near the mirror direction, which is where a highlight appears.

Three light types cover most scenes. Ambient light has no position or direction; it gives a constant base so faces in shadow are not black. A point light has a position; its intensity at distance d falls with attenuation, often 1/(a<sub>0</sub>+a<sub>1</sub>d+a<sub>2</sub>d²), where a<sub>0</sub>,a<sub>1</sub>,a<sub>2</sub> are attenuation constants. A directional light is so far away that all rays are parallel; L is the same everywhere and there is no distance attenuation. Sunlight is treated as directional; a table lamp as point.

The Phong reflection model combines three responses. Ambient is a constant base. Diffuse is light scattered equally from a matte surface; it follows N·L. Specular is the mirror-like highlight; it follows R·V raised to n. The exponent n sets highlight size: small n gives a broad dull spot, large n gives a small sharp spot. k<sub>s</sub> sets highlight strength. Summing over lights allows several lamps.
I = k<sub>a</sub> I<sub>a</sub> + Σ [ k<sub>d</sub> I<sub>l</sub> (N·L) + k<sub>s</sub> I<sub>l</sub> (R·V)<sup>n</sup> ]
blocks.where: I is the final intensity (or colour channel); k<sub>a</sub> is the ambient reflection coefficient; I<sub>a</sub> is ambient light intensity; k<sub>d</sub> is the diffuse coefficient; I<sub>l</sub> is the intensity of light l at the point (includes attenuation for a point light); k<sub>s</sub> is the specular coefficient; N is the unit surface normal; L is the unit vector to the light; R = 2(N·L)N − L; V is the unit vector to the viewer; n is the specular exponent. Use max(0, N·L) and max(0, R·V); the sum is over all lights l.

blocks.text: Use max(0, N·L) and max(0, R·V). If N·L is negative the light is behind the surface and contributes no diffuse term. Normalise N, L, R and V before taking dot products; a non-unit N changes the cosine and the highlight. For a point light, I<sub>l</sub> is reduced by attenuation; for directional light it is not. The ambient term is often added once, not once per light.

Flat shading uses one normal per face, computes one colour and fills the whole polygon with it. It is cheap and correct for a true flat face, but a curved mesh looks faceted. Gouraud shading computes the Phong model at each vertex using that vertex normal, then interpolates the vertex colours along edges and across the polygon. It is cheap and removes most faceting. It cannot create a highlight smaller than the polygon, because no vertex may lie in the highlight. Linear colour interpolation can also produce Mach bands, false bright or dark bands at intensity edges.

Phong shading interpolates the vertex normals across the polygon, normalises the interpolated normal at each pixel, and evaluates the reflection model there. It catches small highlights and gives smooth shading, at the cost of a lighting calculation per pixel. Gouraud needs one lighting calculation per vertex plus interpolation. The table sums the trade-off.
Phong shading is not the Phong reflection model. The first names a per-pixel normal interpolation; the second names the lighting equation used at a point.

figure.caption: The Gouraud path interpolates the vertex intensities 0.2 and 0.6: at the quarter point it gives 0.30. The Phong path normalises normals per pixel, lights the pixel, and sums 0.2, 0.56 and 0.054 to get 0.814.

spec.title: Gouraud vs Phong: worked example
spec.aria: A two-path block diagram: Gouraud interpolates vertex colours from 0.2 and 0.6 to give 0.30 at the quarter point; Phong interpolates normals, lights the pixel, and sums 0.2, 0.56 and 0.054 to give 0.814.

examples.question: A surface point has unit normal N = (0, 0.6, 0.8). A light direction is L = (0, 0, 1). Take k<sub>a</sub> I<sub>a</sub> = 0.2, k<sub>d</sub> = 0.7, I<sub>l</sub> = 1.0, k<sub>s</sub> = 0.5, specular exponent n = 10 and R·V = 0.8. Find the Phong intensity. Also find the Gouraud intensity a quarter of the way along an edge whose vertex intensities are 0.2 and 0.6.
steps: Compute N·L = 0×0 + 0.6×0 + 0.8×1 = 0.80. It is positive, so the diffuse term is active.
Compute 0.8¹⁰ = 0.1074 (to 4 d.p.). Specular term = k<sub>s</sub> I<sub>l</sub> (R·V)¹⁰ = 0.5 × 1.0 × 0.1074 = 0.0537, about 0.054.
examples.answer: The Phong intensity is about 0.814 (dimensionless, in [0,1]); the Gouraud interpolated intensity at the quarter point is 0.30.
examples.check:
NdL = 0.6*0 + 0.8*1
diffuse = 0.7*1.0*NdL
specular = 0.5*1.0*(0.8**10)
total = 0.2 + diffuse + specular
gouraud = 0.2 + 0.25*(0.6-0.2)
print(round(NdL, 3))
print(round(diffuse, 3))
print(round(specular, 3))
print(round(total, 3))
print(round(gouraud, 3))

traps: Expecting Gouraud to show a sharp specular highlight. A highlight smaller than one polygon can fall between vertices and disappear.
Using N or L before normalising. A dot product of non-unit vectors is not a cosine and can exceed 1.
Thinking n changes brightness. n changes the size and falloff of the highlight; k<sub>s</sub> changes its strength.
Using one face normal for all vertices in Gouraud. That gives flat shading, not smooth shading.
Forgetting to clamp negative N·L or R·V to zero; also do not apply distance attenuation to a directional light.

quiz.q: State the difference between Gouraud shading and Phong shading in one sentence.
quiz.a: Gouraud computes lighting at vertices and interpolates colours; Phong interpolates normals, normalises them per pixel and lights each pixel.

quiz.q: Why must N and L be unit vectors before N·L?
quiz.a: Only unit vectors give N·L = cos θ. If they are not unit, the value is scaled by their lengths and is not the cosine used by the lighting equation.

quiz.q: A point has N·L = 0.5, k<sub>d</sub> = 0.8, I<sub>l</sub> = 1.0, ambient k<sub>a</sub> I<sub>a</sub> = 0.1, and no specular. Find I.
For R·V = 0.9, k<sub>s</sub> = 0.4, I<sub>l</sub> = 1.0, compute the specular term for n = 5 and n = 20, and say which highlight is smaller.
Why does Gouraud shading produce Mach bands at a polygon edge?
quiz.a: Colour is interpolated linearly inside each polygon. At an edge the slope of the intensity changes suddenly, and the eye exaggerates this discontinuity as a false bright or dark band.

quiz.q: Compare cost and quality of Gouraud and Phong shading for a shiny sphere on a phone GPU.
quiz.a: Gouraud costs one lighting calculation per vertex and interpolation, so it is cheaper. It smooths the sphere but can miss a small highlight. Phong costs a lighting calculation and a normalisation per pixel; it shows small highlights correctly but uses more work. A phone may choose per-fragment lighting when the highlight matters.

quiz.q: Which method interpolates normals and normalises them per pixel?

beyond: Not for the exam. Real-time engines usually use Blinn-Phong with half-vector H = (L+V)/|L+V|, because H·N replaces R·V and avoids reflecting L. Normal maps store a small normal per texel, so a flat polygon can show bumps under per-pixel lighting. Physically based rendering replaces the three coefficients with material roughness and metalness. Search next: Blinn-Phong, per-fragment lighting, normal mapping, deferred shading, microfacet BRDF.
